messages.subject_clean: Survey design issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am designing a survey based on systematic grid points with a random
starting point. This will allocate survey points to a study area containing
three strata. I can go through the following actions:

Project Browser, Design Tab, Design Details, Properties

However, when I want to move from the General Properties tab to the Effort
Allocation tab it states:

'An unexpected error occurred while checking the options on this page.
Please check they are valid and change any incorrect values.'

.and I am unable to continue.

While designing this survey, a colleague and I have managed to resolve some
of the issues relating to projection and coordinate systems and I am not
sure if it is linked to this. However, in a similar design with similar
problems with the aid of this colleague we were able to go past this problem
and enter the effort as we required. I could not see any difference between
what she had done and the settings of the study area and strata except for
one point: the strata was projected and also had additional project
parameters (which apparently she had not entered herself). The projection
and parameters had to be removed subsequently for mapping for the survey
points, but did not affect the issue above.

Is this problem related to something I have missed in the design, or is it
possibly a problem with my computer? I've looked on the listserv archive and
I can't find anything related to this.

Many thanks in advance

Hugo

messages.subject: Choosing between a truncation of 5% and 10%
messages.subject_clean: Choosing between a truncation of 5% and 10%
messages.body_plain:
Dear authors,

I have been trying to truncate my data from a line-transect study so that=
 they are ready for model selection. I searched the archive and found a m=
essage Len posted back in 2004. He wrote:

"Truncation is not an exact science -- for "good" data, it doesn't make m=
uch difference whether you truncate at 5%, 10% or g(y) approx. 0.15.  I u=
sually try 5%, try 10% and see if either of these fits one less adjustmen=
t term in some "default" model (hn+cos is fine), and then just go with th=
at while keeping an eye on the estimated g(w) and checking it's around 0.=
15ish (this is for line transects).  I often round to some convenient who=
le number (while being aware of any rounding in the data). I prefer less =
truncation to more, all other things being equal. However, there are lots=
 of reasons to use other truncations -- for example, for data with a long=
, flat tail and a short spike in detections close to 0 then more severe t=
runcation can sometimes yield a more reliable result."

I explored my data with hn+cos and uniform+cos, truncating at 5% and 10% =
respectively. For hn+cos, adjustment orders were 2, 3, 4, 5 before trunca=
tion. Both 5% and 10% gave an adjustment of order 2. However, the estimat=
ed g(w) in the 10% scenario was closer to 0.15 than that of the 5% scenar=
io. Please follow the links to view the histograms:

http://img.photobucket.com/albums/v316/qingzhi928/HNcosnotruncation.png
(Histogram of data before truncation; model hn+cos)

http://img.photobucket.com/albums/v316/qingzhi928/HNcostruncation5.png
(Histogram of truncation at 5%; model hn+cos)

http://img.photobucket.com/albums/v316/qingzhi928/HNcostruncation10.png
(Histogram of truncation at 10%; model hn+cos)

For uniform+cos, adjustment orders were 1, 2, 3 before truncation. 5% gav=
e adjustment orders of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 10% gave 1, 2, 3. Is it a bad thing=
 if adjustment orders are the same before and after truncation? I would i=
magine in this case 10% is preferred to 5% because the former had fewer o=
rders, and its estimated g(w) was closer to 0.15?

http://img.photobucket.com/albums/v316/qingzhi928/Unicosnotruncation.png
(Histogram of data before truncation; model uniform+cos)

http://img.photobucket.com/albums/v316/qingzhi928/Unicostruncation5.png
(Histogram of truncation at 5%; model uniform+cos)

http://img.photobucket.com/albums/v316/qingzhi928/Unicostruncation10.png
(Histogram of truncation at 10%; model uniform+cos)

Does it mean that I should go for truncation at 10% for my data because f=
or both models, 10% gave the least adjustment order(s) and an estimated g=
(w) closer to 0.15 than 5%?

Thank you very much for your help.

Regards,
Maria

Hi Eric/list,

I feel a bit responsible here, as I pointed Nicole to the Tweedie option
for her zero-inflated data (before she contacted the DS list). In fact,
in mgcv it is possible to fit the Tweedie distribution - the help is a
bit cryptic as it is not under 'family'; it is under 'Tweedie' (note:
see this within the mgcv, not the Tweedie, package, for a gam example -
copied below). It's not totally straightforward as it's not possible to
fit this distribution within the DSM engine - it can only (at present)
be done within R.

library(mgcv)
set.seed(3)
n<-400
## Simulate data (really Poisson with log-link)
dat <- gamSim(1,n=n,dist="poisson",scale=.2)
## Fit a `nearby' Tweedie...
b <- gam(y~s(x0)+s(x1)+s(x2)+s(x3),family=Tweedie(1.1,power(.1)),data=dat)
plot(b,pages=1)
print(b)
## Same by approximate REML...
b1 <-
gam(y~s(x0)+s(x1)+s(x2)+s(x3),family=Tweedie(1.1,power(.1)),data=dat,method="REML")
plot(b1,pages=1)
print(b1)
rm(dat)

Cheers,
Sharon.

messages.subject: Comparing point and line transects for flying seabirds
messages.subject_clean: Comparing point and line transects for flying seabirds
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

We've been conducting seabird surveys from ships of opportunity in the NW
Atlantic for several years using the snapshot method to count flying birds.
A snapshot for flying birds is conducted roughly once every 300 m along the
track. For the first two years the snapshots were conducted using line
transact methodology - i.e. by recording perpendicular distance from the
line for all birds withing 300m forward of the ship in one of 5 different
categories (A: 0-50m, B: 50-100m, C: 100-200m, D: 200-300m, E: > 300m). The
midpoint of each band is used as the detection distance within Distance (ie.
25, 75, 150, 250m). All dectections in category E (> 300m) are truncated in
the analysis. For the last 1.5 years, we switched to conducting point
transects for the snapshots and measured direct distance to each flying bird
in one of the same 5 categories as for the line transect snapshots, thinking
that it would be easier in the field to estimate direct distance as opposed
to perpendicular distance for birds flying ahead of the ship.

Surveys under each methodology were conducted year-round in the same general
area (eastern Canadian waters) by (mostly) the same observers. Line transect
methodology was employed during 31000 km of transect while the point
transect method was used for about 16000 km.

I now want to compare the results of the two methodologies with the
expectation (or hope) that they would give roughly similar results.  I have
split the data into nine species groups to compare detectability (and
ultimately density) using the two methods. The detection probabilities for
the point transects ranged from 0.15 - 0.35 depending on species.
Surprisingly (to me at least), this was roughly half (or less) of the
corresponding detection probability for the same species under the line
transect method (0.45 - 0.60).  Likewise, the resulting densities were up to
four times lower for the line transect method.

It's been a couple of years since I did the Distance course, so many things
are now cloudy in my mind. So my first question is, should I be able to
compare detection probabilities from the two methods directly? Ie is there
any mathematical reason in the internals of Distance that would make it
invalid to directly compare detection probabilities from the two methods?

I have inspected the detection histograms and fitted functions in an effort
to understand the disparity between the two methods. Most of the histograms
for the line transects look fairly good, with more detections in the closer
distance bands with a gradual decrease towards the more distant categories,
and a half normal function typically fit quite nicely. I have less
experience examining point transect histograms and fitted functions. All
species have between 200 and 1200 detections for the point transect method.
Some (but not all) of the probability density plots appear to have an
over-abundance of detections in the first distance class (0-50m) which I
believe would help explain the low detection probability. But I'm not sure
"how much is too much" and what this would look like on the plot. This is
opposite to what I had expected at the outset. I expected that there would
be an under-abundance of detections in the closest distance class since it
is so small and close to the ship that most species would be reluctanct to
come that close.

Also, some of the fitted detection functions show a "M" shape. Ie. the
fitted line rises over the first two distance classes, falls over the third
one, rises again over the fourth before trailing off. This I interpret to be
either too few detections in the third class or too many in the fourth. Does
this make sense? I realize that point counts are more sensitive in general
to violation of assumptions (e.g. accurate distance measurement, lack of
evasive movement by the birds), but I don't have a feel how much these can
be violated nor what these violations might look like in a probability
density plot.

I have looked at the curves and histograms for individual observers and note
a fair amount of variation but many of them do not have enough detections to
draw any conclusions.

Has anyone else compared line and point transect methodologies directly? Can
you think of anything I'm missing?

Thanks for your help!
Dave
--
Dave Fifield
da...@mun.ca

Dave, that is an interesting study - it would be good to know the
reasons for the differences, so that recommendations on which approach
to use can be made.

My own prejudice is that the point transect method will be less robust,
with estimates more sensitive to failures of assumption.  The 'M' shaped
curve for f(r) would tend to support that conclusion.  (You say det fn,
but I think you mean the pdf?  By default, Distance constrains the det
fn so it can't increase, even if the data suggest it should.)   However,
there is likely to be a g(0) issue for the line transect method.  Thoughts:

1. It may be that the odd shape is caused by bias in estimating
distances - but why would this be an issue for point transects and not
line transects?

2.  It may be that one peak corresponds to detections made by naked eye,
and the other to detections made with the aid of binoculars.

3.  The snapshot method is an attempt to avoid bias arising from
(non-responsive) movement.  Of course, in practice, the snapshot isn't
just an instant in time.  You have to spend time searching for birds and
recording their positions.  This gives time for movement, and will
create bias towards recording birds too close to the observer, when they
become more detectable.  This will bias point transect methods more than
line transect methods, as birds might be moving either towards the line
or away from it, when they become close enough to the observer to be
detected.  Also, a small number of birds recorded too close to the
observer will have a large effect on point transect estimates, because
relatively few detections occur close to the point.  By contrast, there
is a much higher proportion of detections in the first bin for line
transect sampling, so recording a few birds as closer to the point than
they should have been has a smaller effect - especially when 'closer to
the point' doesn't necessarily equate to 'closer to the line'.

4.  The one reason I can think of that might cause the line transect
estimates to be biased low is that you're assuming g(0)=1.  But you're
searching up to 300m from the observer along the line.  Hence you will
miss birds in the first bin - and you will miss more birds in that bin
than would be the case if g(0)=1.  If you were prepared to assume that
the same det fn applies along the line as perpendicular to the line, you
can estimate that g(0)=P_a - which you say ranges between 0.45 and 0.6.
This would result in a doubling of your line transect estimates.

So my expectation is that the point transect method overestimates
density due to movement issues, while the line transect method
underestimates, because g(0)<1.

I haven't encountered this snapshot approach to line transect sampling
before.  If you can extend it to allow estimation of g(0), I think this
could be a useful method.  Not sure if the correction I suggest above is
likely to be good enough.

Steve Buckland

> > It's been a couple of years since I did the Distance course, so many things
> > are now cloudy in my mind. So my first question is, should I be able to
> > compare detection probabilities from the two methods directly? Ie is there
> > any mathematical reason in the internals of Distance that would make it
> > invalid to directly compare detection probabilities from the two methods?
> >
> > I have inspected the detection histograms and fitted functions in an effort
> > to understand the disparity between the two methods. Most of the histograms
> > for the line transects look fairly good, with more detections in the closer
> > distance bands with a gradual decrease towards the more distant categories,
> > and a half normal function typically fit quite nicely. I have less
> > experience examining point transect histograms and fitted functions. All
> > species have between 200 and 1200 detections for the point transect method.
> > Some (but not all) of the probability density plots appear to have an
> > over-abundance of detections in the first distance class (0-50m) which I

> > "how much is too much" and what this would look like on the plot. This is
> > opposite to what I had expected at the outset. I expected that there would
> > be an under-abundance of detections in the closest distance class since it
> > is so small and close to the ship that most species would be reluctanct to
> > come that close.
> >

> > fitted line rises over the first two distance classes, falls over the third

Chandra:

Look at the Properties associated by default with the Coverage layer you
are trying to create.  There will be a default spacing of the grid
points.  Distance is reporting that the spacing is too coarse for any
points to fit within the specified (by the shape file) study region
boundary.

Specifying the spacing is an iterative process in Distance; recall you
are essentially going to overwrite the coverage layer that you are
asking Distance to manufacture by the prediction grid that you have
constructed with your GIS.  If my advice confuses you even further, send
your project along to me, and I can have a look next week (after we
finish our workshops here in St. Andrews).
